moving on to information items policy 8230 appeals and hearing miss scanlon yes thank you we are bringing to you today recommended revisions to policy 8230 which will include a recommended revision actually to the title of the policy to procedures for student disciplinary hearings to the school board this of course is the policy that governs when a student or parent parent can appeal to either SBAC or the full board and how those appeals will progress.

While the red line would reveal a lot of changes, most, the vast majority of those changes were made for clarity and precision of language and also to ensure that the words used did align with the Code of Virginia.

That said, there were some substantive changes to the policy that I would like to highlight you and then I would be happy to take any questions that you have so the first substantive change that I would highlight is actually in lines two to three this revised policy explicitly names SBAC your committee as the three member committee which will consider student disciplinary appeals this is in accordance with policy 2310 committees of the school board previously the policy

referenced a three-member committee of the board, but didn't explicitly note that SBAC is that committee. Moving on to lines 4 through 5, as required by the Code of Virginia, in addition to allowing for an appeal of a long-term suspension and expulsion recommendation, the revised policy also provides for an appeal to SBAC of any exclusion or reassignment decision. The prior policy did not explicitly note that exclusion and reassignment decisions could be appealed

to SBAC, but the code requires that appeal, so we have been doing those appeals even though they weren't explicitly noted in the policy, so that is something that's just meant to better align us with the Code of Virginia. Further, we chose the word reassignment to allow an appeal of any reassignment decision.

That would include an appeal of a reassignment decision to a comprehensive school, a different comprehensive school, as well as an appeal to an alternative education setting. The code only requires that we provide an appeal of a reassignment if that reassignment is to an alternative education setting.

But staff is recommending that we also afford an appeal of a reassignment to a different comprehensive school, just because that is a significant decision were it to occur, and it would be reasonable to permit a student or a parent, in our view, to appeal that decision.
Lines 7 through 9, the revised policy limits the scope of SBAC's authority to affirming, modifying, or annulling the sanction.

The revised policy does not permit SBAC to modify or annul the finding that the student violated the rules. So what would be at play would not be did the student violate the rules, but was that sanction appropriate given the violation.

The reason that we are recommending that change is, first, that does align us with the Code of Virginia. The Code of Virginia permits parents or students to appeal sanctions. It does not explicitly permit an appeal of the finding itself that the rules were violated.

So that's the first rationale. Secondly, the finding was made typically by the assistant principal. It was affirmed by the principal. It was affirmed, again, by the hearing officer, who is a highly trained, impartial representative of the division superintendent.

And so by the time a case appears before SBAC, that decision has been affirmed. the finding that the student violated the rules has been affirmed at least twice, if not three times, including through an impartial hearings process.

As such, staff does not believe that it would be necessary to revisit the finding. The third reason that we are recommending that this change occur is that were you to consider an appeal of a decision that was made under Title IX, The federal regulations implementing Title IX would not permit you to even consider the finding.

You would, however, have the authority to modify, affirm, or annul the sanction. So since you absolutely cannot, under those federal regulations with a Title IX case, modify or annul the finding, staff believes that having two different processes for different types of cases would be confusing and not best practice moving on then to lines 88 through 89

the revised policy does state that only division counsel would be present with s back during your deliberations so when s back has a hearing both sides are presented the parties exit the room and you deliberate on what the appropriate decision is, this policy would provide that the only person permitted in the room during your deliberations would be division counsel.

The current policy does provide for the director of OSA to be part of those deliberations, but given that the director of OSA is, in a sense, a party to the decision, there could be an appearance of impropriety for the director to be with you during deliberations, which is why we recommend that change.

Finally, in lines 143 through 144, the revised policy makes it clear that if there is an appeal of SBAC's decision to the full board, that the full board would consider that appeal on the written record unless the chair of the board opts to schedule a hearing before the full board.

So appeals can only go beyond SBAC to the full board if your decision is not unanimous. If you make a unanimous decision as a committee, then that is the final decision on the part of the school system.

But if your decision was two to one against what the family or student wishes, the family does have one more appeal to the full board. The Code of Virginia only provides the right to appeal to the full board on the written record, and we recommend that that's what we afford our families unless there is an exigent circumstance that would leave the chair to say there should be a hearing.

We did do some pretty significant revisions to Regulation 8240. We started many, many months ago. It was many months in the making. was a very collaborative process.

Of course, the policy defines terms and also defines what is prohibited. The regulation sets forth the sanctions for various kinds of violations. So we wanted to revise the regulation with the following goals in mind.

First and foremost, student safety. Also, ensuring that student safety doesn't come at the cost of continuing to provide education and intervention services for students. We recognize those have to go hand in hand.
We wanted to therefore balance intervention with accountability and we wanted to provide flexibility to our principals to respond to the most serious violations, in particular fentanyl.

So in terms of the process, as I said, it was very collaborative. We did have meetings with school-based administrators that were attended by the entire OSA team. I believe Mr. Madison was present at the big meeting. I know that Jennifer Evans was present.

Several meetings of the OSA team and Mr. Madison and Ms. Evans to really hammer out and revise and look at the regulation itself. We then conducted a focus group that included ten secondary principals, five middle and five high school principals, where we went through that regulation really almost line by line to get their feedback and make sure that the adjustments we were making made sense for them in the schools.

We didn't include the elementary school principals here. Well, they were included in the general, the first meetings, but not in the focus group, really primarily because the vast majority of the violations that we see coming through OSA and those that occur are happening at the middle and the high school level.

So that was why we focused on the secondary school principals. Once we had received their feedback, we then reviewed it thoroughly, again, almost line by line with the Department of School leadership, Dossel, and certainly it was reviewed by Cabinet and also reviewed by Division Council.

The highlights, some of the changes that were made, first, the new regulation did provide for a two-year look back. So essentially, the previous regulation was silent to this, but the practice had been on the first day of school every year sort of the clock reset so when the regulations set forth your first violation this will happen your second violation this will happen your third violation

this will happen in practice what was occurring is a student might have two three four five six 82 40 violations in a school year right up until June and then the first day of school would come and it would be back to zero, and we recognized that that was not the best approach. We also did not want to go way back to ancient history on a student and say, well, you know, four years ago you had a tobacco vape, so we tried to strike a balance how far back in the record should our

administrators look to determine what violation is this really, right, because if you had five in June. And then August comes, it's not your first violation. And we settled on 24 months. So anytime there is an 8240 violation, the principal or assistant principal will look back 24 months and see how many violations occurred in those 24 months to determine are we at a first violation, a second violation, a third violation, et cetera. So that was a change. Another change
was that the range of consequences that a student would receive except for a distribution, distribution, first offense, it's going to come forward when we have drugs being distributed at school.

So that is an outlier. But essentially what was happening in practice with the former regulation was if there was a tobacco violation, you might have two tobacco violations in the same school year, And then a student would have an alcohol violation.

And it was like, well, two tobaccos, but now this is your first time alcohol. And then there might be three alcohol violations. And then there was a THC violation. And that would be the first violation. Instead of saying, well, wait a minute. It's not that we want to respond with progressive services and progressive discipline for every single category of substance.

But rather, a violation is a violation is a violation. So they look back the two years, and it doesn't matter if those violations were nicotine, marijuana, controlled substance, alcohol. They total those violations up in those preceding 24 months to determine what violation are we on now, and then how do we proceed in terms of the consequence.

Another highlight is that, again, in the interest of providing intervention services and supports to our students, typically a violation related to over-the-counter medication, use or possession of one's own prescription medication, a tobacco violation, including a nicotine vape, an alcohol violation, or a drug paraphernalia violation will result in school-based discipline.

Another change or revision was that typically, except for cases, again, involving drug distribution, a student's first violation of the policy within the 24 months would be responded to, again, with an in-school consequence and a substance use education class.

At two or more violations, that's when the school would have the ability to suspend if they felt that was appropriate and to refer to OSA for further disciplinary action if they felt that was appropriate. However, offenses involving distribution must result in a 10-day suspension or referral to OSA to consider further disciplinary action.

And then finally, the substance use class is now being not only offered, but required with every violation. And we clarified that the expectation would be that if the student is in an in-school restriction setting, that preferably we want to have that substance use education component provided to the student while they are in ISR, so that they're not then taken out of class again to get their substance use education component.
